prompt: Which three things make up a case? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The input, exactly as the program sends it
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: The expected output, decided by a person
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: How to judge a reply against it
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: The model's score on a public benchmark
choices.why: That is somebody else's case.

prompt: A model scores well on a public benchmark and writes 'Refund.' where ana's program expects `refund`. Which of section 02's reasons does that illustrate?

choices.text: The questions are not hers
choices.why: The question here is hers; the trouble is the form of the answer.

choices.text: The labels are not hers
choices.why: The label chosen is right; it is written differently.

choices.text: The format is not hers
choices.why: Right. Her program parses the reply, and a benchmark grading meaning would pass it.

choices.text: The benchmark was measured in another language entirely
choices.why: Language is not what goes wrong here.

prompt: Why did ana keep fifteen cases with no order number in them?
hint: What answer would never be tested otherwise?

choices.text: To make the extraction task easier
choices.why: They test the answer a sloppy model gets wrong.

choices.text: So the set tests the answer 'there is none'
choices.why: Right, and section 09 found an invented value on exactly such a case.

choices.text: Because the inbox has exactly that share of them
choices.why: The set was balanced, not mirrored.

choices.text: Because sorting needs them to reach five labels
choices.why: Labels and missing orders are independent.

prompt: Two people label the same cases independently and cannot agree on one. What does section 03 say about that case?
hint: Can a model be scored fairly on it?

choices.text: Keep it, and let the best model decide the label
choices.why: That is the evaluation grading itself.

choices.text: Count it as right for every model
choices.why: That inflates every score equally and teaches nothing.

choices.text: Rewrite it, rule on it, or remove it
choices.why: Right. No model can be scored fairly on a case people do not agree on.

choices.text: Average the two labels
choices.why: Labels are categories; there is no average.

prompt: A reply is 'refund.' and the label is `refund`. How does section 04 score it?

choices.text: Right on both
choices.why: Strict compares character for character.

choices.text: Wrong strict, right loose
choices.why: Right. The model chose correctly and wrote it untidily.

choices.text: Right strict, wrong loose
choices.why: Loose is the more forgiving of the two.

choices.text: Wrong on both
choices.why: Loose drops the full stop.

prompt: Why does section 04 not use another model to judge the sorting replies?

choices.text: Because models refuse to grade other models' work
choices.why: They do not refuse; the point is they are not needed.

choices.text: Because a judge would always agree with the model being judged
choices.why: Not always; its errors may correlate, which is a different claim.

choices.text: A program checks a label more cheaply and reliably
choices.why: Right. Judging by model is for open-ended output, and is itself checked.

choices.text: Because judging is forbidden by the providers' terms
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

prompt: Match each reply, for a case whose order is LB-20452, to how `score_extract` scores it.
hint: Does the whole reply parse? Does a `{...}` inside it?

prompt: Why does the harness write the raw answer to the run file, and not only the score?

choices.text: Rescoring then costs no new requests
choices.why: Right, and a dispute about a case is settled by reading what was written.

choices.text: The provider requires a copy of every answer
choices.why: No provider requires it.

choices.text: Raw answers are needed to compute tokens
choices.why: Tokens come from the usage the API returns.

choices.text: To train the next model on them
choices.why: That is not what an evaluation is for.

prompt: The harness sends every candidate the same messages, max_tokens and temperature. What would go wrong if one candidate got a different temperature?

choices.text: Nothing; temperature only affects speed
choices.why: It affects which answer comes out.

choices.text: The request would be refused
choices.why: Different temperatures are valid requests.

choices.text: The token counts could not be compared
choices.why: Counts are comparable; the answers are what change.

choices.text: Its score would mix in the setting
choices.why: Right. Section 08 saw four answers move on temperature alone.

prompt: qwen2.5:3b sorted 30 of 40 correctly. As a percentage, what is that score?
qwen2.5:3b's 95% interval and llama3.2:3b's overlap, from 60% to 63%. What does that say?

choices.text: The two are equally good
choices.why: Overlap does not show equality; it fails to show a difference.

choices.text: The intervals alone do not settle which is better
choices.why: Right. The paired comparison asks the sharper question, and it does settle it.

choices.text: The harness has a bug
choices.why: Wide intervals are what forty cases give.

choices.text: The higher score should be ignored
choices.why: It is the best estimate, with its uncertainty stated.

prompt: Only qwen2.5:3b was right on 16 cases and only llama3.2:3b on 5. What does the 0.027 on the last line say?

choices.text: That qwen2.5:3b is right 2.7% more often
choices.why: It is a probability about the split, not a difference in accuracy.

choices.text: That a split this uneven would be rare if they were equally good
choices.why: Right: about three times in a hundred, under the one in twenty convention.

choices.text: That 27 of the 40 cases agreed
choices.why: The cases where both agreed do not enter the calculation.

choices.text: That the interval is 60% to 86%
choices.why: The interval is a separate calculation.

prompt: Five cases are wrong for all three models. What does section 07 say to suspect first?

choices.text: The prompt
choices.why: Possible, but the pattern points elsewhere first.

choices.text: The label
choices.why: Right. Here both labels stood when they were looked at again, with a reason.

choices.text: Ollama's server
choices.why: The server answered every request.

choices.text: The scoring rule
choices.why: Strict and loose agree on these cases.

prompt: Match each failure to its group in section 07.

pairs.left: 'refund' for a parcel marked delivered that never came
'I can't do that' for a request to delete an account
'order-status' as nineteen of twenty-one wrong answers

prompt: Why is changing a label only because the models disagreed with it a problem?
hint: What would the score then measure?

choices.text: The evaluation would be grading itself
choices.why: Right. A label changes for a reason a person accepts, recorded with it.

choices.text: Labels may never change once written
choices.why: They may, with a reason; section 07 changed one.

choices.text: It would make the scores lower
choices.why: It would make them higher, which is the danger.

choices.text: Models are usually right about labels
choices.why: The shop decides what its labels mean.

prompt: At which temperature should ana run classification and extraction?

choices.text: 1, so the model can consider alternatives
choices.why: Variety is only noise when there is one right answer.
Right. Section 08's rerun at 0 matched case for case.

choices.text: Whatever the provider sets by default
choices.why: Defaults differ between providers, so the comparison would not be fair.

choices.text: A different one per model, tuned for its best score
choices.why: Then the scores would measure the tuning.

prompt: Two runs of qwen2.5:3b at temperature 1 scored 29 and 30 loose. In how many cases did their answers differ?
One model's runs differ by two cases at temperature 1; two models differ by three. What does section 08 conclude?
hint: Compare the gap with the noise.

choices.text: The second model is better by three cases
choices.why: A gap close to one model's own spread is not a difference.

choices.text: Temperature 1 is better because it explores more
choices.why: Exploring adds noise to a task with one answer.

choices.text: The gap is about the size of the noise
choices.why: Right. Run more than once before calling a difference.

choices.text: Evaluations at temperature 1 are invalid
choices.why: They are valid if the spread is reported.

prompt: llama3.2:1b found the right order 12 times when the program fished it out of the text, but only 8 times as clean JSON. What kind of failure is the gap?
hint: The number inside was right four more times.

choices.text: A content failure, which a larger prompt fixes
choices.why: The content was right in those four.

choices.text: Format, which a schema or a tidying step addresses
choices.why: Right. Either moves the strict score towards the loose one.

choices.text: A scoring bug, because strict is too harsh
choices.why: The strict rule is what the program does.

choices.text: A labelling error in the cases
choices.why: The cases' order numbers were right.

prompt: Which of these extraction errors would a program that looks the number up be least likely to notice?
hint: Which one is in the shop's own format?

choices.text: `null` for an e-mail that names LB-20417
choices.why: A missing order is noticed: the reply asks for it again.

choices.text: `SMH-IL-12345` for a question about an edition
choices.why: That is not an order number the shop could have.

choices.text: `LB-12345` for an e-mail that names no order
choices.why: Right: it is in the shop's format, and one day it is somebody's order.
The suffix makes it a number no order has.

prompt: What rule decides among candidates, per task, in section 10?

choices.text: The highest score, whatever it costs
choices.why: Above the floor, price ranks.

choices.text: The same model for every task, for simplicity
choices.why: Tasks have different floors and different winners.

choices.text: The cheapest that passes every floor
choices.why: Right, one task at a time.

choices.text: The newest model from the largest provider
choices.why: Neither newness nor size is a criterion.

prompt: Put the life of an evaluation in order.
hint: From writing cases to the next model.
items: Choose, and keep the run as a baseline
Gate every later change against it
trap: The baseline is kept at the moment of choosing; without it nothing later can be gated.

prompt: A comparison that fails a run with exit status 1 when the score drops too far is called a ___ in evalkit.
A new version of the chosen model is released. What does ana do, by this lesson's method?
hint: A change to one input of the evaluation.

choices.text: Switch, since newer versions are better
choices.why: Newer is a claim; the cases test it.

choices.text: Ignore it until the old one is retired
choices.why: Waiting means evaluating under a deadline.

choices.text: Read its model card and decide from the benchmarks
choices.why: Benchmarks measure somebody else's task.

choices.text: Run her cases on it and gate against the baseline
choices.why: Right: an afternoon, because the evaluation was already written.
